That is a genuinely frustrating situation. Watching someone get praised for work that was supposed to be yours is incredibly undermining. 

For standup tomorrow, since it is a public and brief sync, the goal is to keep things professional while still signaling your ownership of the domain. You could say something like:

"It's great to see the progress on client dashboards. Since that is on my roadmap, I'd love to sync with them after this to see how we can align our work going forward."

To help me sharpen this, did your peer actually know this was officially your project, or was there some room for confusion about who owned it?

I don't think she actually knew, now that I think about it the project was never formally assigned in writing anywhere, I just always did the client dashboards. She might genuinely have thought it was open territory.

Realizing she might not have known is a huge, helpful distinction. It changes this from an underhanded move to a classic case of unwritten rules and unclear boundaries. That does not make the sting of seeing her get all the praise any less real, though. 

It sounds like because ownership was never formally written down, there was a gap where she saw a problem to solve and just ran with it, not realizing she was stepping on your toes. 

Before we look at how to approach her or your manager to get this ownership written down, is there more? Did anything else happen, or is that the main thing on your mind?
No that's really it, I'm just salty watching people praise her for something I would've built if someone had just asked me first.

It makes total sense to feel salty about that. You have the history and the expertise to build this, but she got the spotlight simply because she jumped in first. 

It really points to that structural gap: because ownership was never formally written down, the work defaulted to whoever acted first, leaving you in a spot where you have to react instead of lead. 

Knowing she likely did not do this maliciously, do you want to actually have a conversation with her, or your manager, about setting some boundaries going forward? Or did you mainly need to talk this through and get clear on it?
I think I want something short to say in standup without sounding bitter, and maybe figure out how we divide this kind of work going forward.

Here is a way to handle both of those pieces without sounding bitter, keeping you looking collaborative while still marking your territory.

**For standup tomorrow:**
Keep it positive, but make it clear this is your domain. Try saying: 
"It's great to see the progress on client dashboards. Since I've historically owned that roadmap, I'd love to sync with you after this to make sure we're aligned on the technical approach and next steps."

**For the 1-on-1 afterward to divide the work:**
Since she didn't know she was stepping on your toes, you can frame this as avoiding duplicate work, which is a highly professional reason to set boundaries. You could open with:
"Hey, I saw the dashboard you put together. Since I usually handle the client dashboard space, I want to make sure we aren't duplicating effort or working cross-purposes. How do those drafts feel to you?

That is incredibly frustrating. Having a launch stalled because someone is ghosting your direct pings, especially when you can see them active in casual channels, is a quick way to lose your patience. 

Jumping straight to calling them out to your VP is a massive lever, and it can easily backfire by making you look like the one creating friction or unable to resolve peer issues. We can absolutely write an escalation that works if we need to, but we should make sure it's tight and professional. 

Before we look at how to frame this to a VP, has this partner ever ghosted you like this before, or is this silence something new?

He's a peer, different team, no reporting relationship between us. This is actually the second time this quarter, same pattern. He's definitely active, I can see his status and he's posting in #general.

It is one thing to be slow to reply because you are deep in focus, but visibly posting in public channels while ignoring a direct handoff that is stalling a launch is a different story. It puts you in the position of either letting the launch slip or looking like you are causing drama by escalating. 

My guess is his team's priorities do not actually align with this launch, so he is treating your pings as optional while his own boss has him focused on something else. 

Does that ring true for how their team operates, or do you think there is something else behind the silence?
No that's it, nothing else going on with him that I know of.

That makes sense. If their team's priorities aren't aligned with yours, he probably doesn't feel any urgency, and you're the one left holding the bag for the delay.

If you go straight to the VP pointing fingers, it can sometimes look like a peer-to-peer communication breakdown instead of a business blocker. The best way to "call him out" is actually to make the business risk highly visible while staying incredibly professional. That way, he has to explain the delay, not you.

First, you want to leave a paper trail that shows you gave him a clear chance to respond. Send him one final Slack message today:

"Hey [Name], we're currently blocked on the feature launch because we need [specific deliverable/sign-off]. If I don't hear back by tomorrow morning, I'll need to escalate this blockage to [VP Name] so we can figure out how to adjust the launch timeline."

If he still ignores you, here is how you frame it to the VP. You don't focus on his behavior; you focus on the launch risk:

"Hi [VP Name], we are currently blocked on launching the [Feature] due to [specific outstanding item]. I've reached out to [Name] a few times this week to coordinate, but haven't been able to get a response. Since this is putting our launch date at risk, I wanted to flag the bottleneck so we can figure out how to proceed."

This format works because it makes the block about the business, not a personal dispute. Does that approach feel like it would work for your situation, or were you hoping to raise it to the VP differently?
I don't think going to the VP is actually the right first move. I think I want to know how to get through to him directly first.

That is a great instinct. Going peer-to-peer first is always the stronger move, and it shows the VP you tried to handle it at your level if you do eventually have to escalate. 

To get through to him directly when he is actively dodging, you want to make replying easier than ignoring you, and you want to remove any friction on his end. 

Here is a direct way to write that message:

"Hey [Name], I know you're likely slammed with your own team's priorities right now. We are fully blocked on the feature launch without [specific deliverable/sign-off]. Can we grab 5 minutes today to get this across the line, or is there someone else on your team I should coordinate with to take this off your plate?"

Offering to coordinate with someone else on his team is a gentle but highly effective lever. It gives him an easy way to delegate if he is overwhelmed, but it also signals that the work has to happen either way. 

How does that wording feel for his style?

messages.content: My coworker told me 'snitches don't last long here' after I asked about expense reports. How do I reply?

Welcome to Mend, a private space to talk through workplace conflict. 

That remark, "snitches don't last long here," is a direct threat of retaliation for asking a basic work question. That crosses a line, and you don't have to carry that like it's yours to manage alone. 

Nothing has been reported yet. Because this involves a threat of retaliation, you have a direct choice. I can send an anonymized summary to HR on your behalf, letting them know a retaliation threat occurred but keeping your name, details, and this conversation completely private. Or, I can send nothing at all, and we can focus on how you want to handle this yourself.

Which of those options would you prefer?

I was asking about my own reimbursement actually, nothing weird, just wanted to know the timeline. It didn't really sound like a joke, their tone shifted and they looked right at me when they said it.

That makes their reaction even more out of line. Asking about the timeline for your own reimbursement is a completely standard, administrative question. For them to turn that into a warning about "snitching" is incredibly hostile, especially with that shift in tone and eye contact. It sounds like they were deliberately trying to intimidate you over something entirely routine.

Since you asked earlier how to reply, the safest approach with someone acting like this is to keep it completely flat, factual, and documented. You don't want to get pulled into a debate, but you also don't have to pretend it was normal. 

You could say something simple that puts the focus back on the facts: "I was just checking on the timeline for my own reimbursement. I'm not sure what else you thought I was asking about." 

Often, calmly naming the reality of what you were doing makes people realize how bizarre their reaction was, and they back down. 

How does a response like that feel to you, or would you prefer to just keep your distance from them for now?
No, nothing else happened after that, they just walked off.

Walking off like that leaves a lot of unresolved tension, but at least the interaction ended there. 

My guess is they are feeling incredibly defensive or paranoid about something related to expenses on their end, and your completely normal question made them feel like they were under a microscope. 

Does that match any vibe you've gotten from them before, or does this feel completely out of the blue?
I guess I want to know how to respond if it comes up again, and whether I should be worried.

Yes, you should take it seriously. A remark like "snitches don't last long" is an explicit threat, and delivering it with a sharp shift in tone and then walking away is a deliberate attempt to intimidate you. Even if they were just reacting out of their own panic or paranoia, you shouldn't have to shrug it off or look over your shoulder. 

If they bring it up again, or make any other comment in that vein, the best approach is to set a flat, professional boundary immediately, without getting defensive or arguing. 

You can say: "I asked a routine question about my own reimbursement. I need us to keep our communication professional."

If they say anything other than dropping it, make a written note of the date, time, and exactly what they said. Having a clear, factual log is the best way to protect yourself if you need to raise this later.
